what: Caris Life Sciences analyses tumours. It runs laboratory tests that sequence a cancer patient’s tumour to identify the specific genetic changes driving it, which tells the oncologist which treatments are likely to work. It also builds a database from those results used by pharmaceutical companies for drug development.
customers: Oncologists ordering molecular profiling for cancer patients, with payment from insurers and Medicare, plus pharmaceutical companies buying access to the resulting data and research services.
money: Comprehensive tumour sequencing and analysis ordered by treating physicians.
Research partnerships and access to the clinical and molecular database.
moat: Each test performed adds a tumour profile paired with the patient’s subsequent treatment and outcome to a database that cannot be assembled any other way. That dataset makes the interpretation better, which makes oncologists more likely to order the test, which grows the dataset. Pharmaceutical companies pay for access, which turns the test volume into a second revenue stream.
risks: The company listed recently, with revenue history available only from 2023 and no record through a reimbursement change.
Reimbursement rates for molecular profiling are set by insurers and Medicare and could be reduced, which would affect the entire business at once.
Thirteen analysts average a $34.23 target against an $18.54 price, an 85% gap reflecting very different views on a short-history company.
Free cash flow of only $28.9M against $96.1M of net income, and 30.7 times EV/EBITDA, mean the valuation rests on growth continuing.
Tempus AI and Guardant Health are pursuing the same oncologists with similar propositions and substantial funding.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $306.1M in 2023 to $812.0M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.0B.
Cash of $798.6M against $427.7M of debt is a strong net cash position for a company at this stage.
The database grows with every test and cannot be replicated retrospectively by a competitor.
Precision oncology is becoming standard practice, so the proportion of cancer patients profiled keeps rising.
Pharmaceutical data partnerships monetise the same test volume a second time at very high margins.
watch: Test volumes and revenue per test, plus the pharmaceutical data revenue separately. Volume builds the database, reimbursement determines whether it pays, and the data business is where the margin is.
view: Caris sits in one of the better structural positions in diagnostics, and the reason is the feedback loop rather than the test itself. Sequencing a tumour is technically demanding but increasingly commoditised. What is not replicable is the accumulated record of tumour profiles paired with what treatment the patient received and what happened next. Every test adds to it, better data makes the interpretation more useful, more useful interpretation brings more orders, and pharmaceutical companies pay for access to the whole thing. A competitor starting today cannot buy that history.

The growth reflects a real shift in oncology practice. Molecular profiling has moved from a specialist curiosity to something close to standard of care, because treatment selection increasingly depends on which mutations are driving the tumour. Revenue from $306 million in 2023 to $1.0 billion trailing is that adoption happening, and cash of $799 million against $428 million of debt means the company can fund it.

The risk that would damage every company in this field simultaneously is reimbursement. Insurers and Medicare set what a molecular profile pays, those rates have been generous relative to the falling cost of sequencing, and that gap is exactly the kind of thing payers eventually address. A reduction would hit revenue immediately and across the whole industry, and no amount of competitive positioning protects against it.

The competition is also serious and well funded: Tempus AI and Guardant Health are pursuing the same oncologists with similar data-flywheel arguments. At 30.7 times EV/EBITDA with free cash flow of only $29 million against $96 million of net income, the price assumes Caris wins a meaningful share and that reimbursement holds. The thirteen analysts averaging 85% above the price reflect how early this is. Test volumes, revenue per test and the pharmaceutical data line separately are what I would follow; the consolidated revenue hides which engine is actually running.
bull: Molecular profiling becomes standard for most cancer patients, the outcomes database compounds into an unmatched asset, and pharmaceutical data partnerships monetise it at high margin.
bear: Payers cut reimbursement for tumour profiling as sequencing costs fall, Tempus and Guardant split the market, and a 31 times EV/EBITDA multiple on a short record corrects.
